ety.text: From Middle English paun, pawyn, pawnd, from Old French pan, pant (“pledge for a payment”), from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *pand (“deposit, security, pledge”), further origin uncertain. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Pound (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), West Frisian pân (“pawn”), Dutch pand (“pledge, pawn”), German Low German Pand (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), German Pfand (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), Swedish pant (“pledge, pawn”), Faroese pantur (“security, lien”), Icelandic pantur (“pledge, security, pawn”).
From Middle English pown, from Anglo-Norman poun, paun (“footman”), from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”), derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Doublet of peon.

senses.d: The state of being held as security for a loan, or as a pledge.
ex: All our jewellery was in pawn by this stage.
Redeem from broking pawn the blemish'd crown.
As therefore the morning devv, is a pavvne of the evenings fatneſſe, ſo, O Lord, let this daies comfort be the earneſt of to morrowes, […]

senses.d: An item given as security on a loan, or as a pledge.
ex: My life I never held but as a pawn / To wage against thy enemies.
Brokers, takers of pawns, biting userers, I will not admit; yet […] I will tolerate some kind of usery.

senses.d: To pledge; to stake or wager.
To give as security on a loan of money; especially, to deposit (something) at a pawn shop.
ex: But you'd better take your diamond ring, you'd better pawn it, babe.

senses.d: The most numerous chess piece, or a similar piece in a similar game. In chess, each side starts with eight; moves are only forward, and attacks are only diagonally or en passant.
A person being manipulated by another, being used to some end.
ex: Though a pawn of the gods, her departure is the precipitating cause of the Trojan War.

grp.label: (rare) type of shop — see also pawnshop
item sold to a pawn shop

pt:topa-tudo.gl: Someone who will do anything for money.

ety.text: From topa (“accepts”) + tudo (“everything”).
Portuguese penhorardeverb. Portuguese penhora Deverbal from penhorar.
From Latin in pignus.
Inherited from Middle French gage, from Old French gage, guage, from Early Medieval Latin wadius (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Frankish *waddī.

chain.g: to pawn, make a pledge, plight

ety.text: From Middle French engager, from Old French engagier (“to pawn, make a pledge, plight”), from en- (“in, under”) + gage, guage (“pledge”), from Late Latin wadium (“pledge”), from Frankish *wadi ~ waddj- (“pledge”), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge, guarantee”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“guarantee, bail”).

es:empeñar.gl: to pawn, to hock (sell something to a pawn shop)

ety.text: From empeño + -ar.
Inherited from Latin pignorāre.
Inherited from Late Latin *impignāre, from pignus (“pledge”). Compare Spanish empeñar and Italian impegnare.
Inherited from Old French peon, from Late Latin pedōnem, derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Doublet of péon, which was borrowed from Spanish peón.
Inherited from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”), derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Compare French pion. Doublet of peone, borrowed from Spanish peón.
Cf. pedone.
Inherited from Late Latin pedōnem (“footsoldier”), from Latin pedem (“foot”). Compare Portuguese peão, French pion, Italian pedone.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese peon, an early semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pedōnem (“one who goes on foot”), from Latin pēs (“foot”). Compare Galician peón, Spanish peón, French pion, Italian pedone.

From Middle English pawe, from Old French poue, poe, from Vulgar Latin *pauta. Further origin unknown, perhaps from Frankish *pōta, from Frankish *pōtōn (“to put, stick, plant”), from Proto-Germanic *putōną, whence also Old English potian (“to push”), pȳtan (“to put out, poke out”). See more at put. Doublet of pote, put, and putt. Cognate with Dutch poot, poten (“to plant”), Low German Pote, German Pfote, Icelandic pota (“to stick”).

senses.d: The soft foot of a mammal or other animal, generally a quadruped, that has claws or nails; comparable to a human hand or foot.

ex: Get your grubby paws off my things!
Abel smiled broadly and proffered his hamlike paw to the chief […]

senses.d: Of an animal, to dig through (something, such as a garbage can) with paws.
Of an animal, to draw the forefoot along the ground; to beat or scrape with the forefoot.
ex: He paweth in the valley, and rejoiceth in his strength: he goeth on to meet the armed men.

senses.d: To touch (someone) in a sexual way.

ety.text: From Middle French, from Old French pade, pate (“paw, foot of an animal”), from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”), borrowed from Frankish *patta (“paw, sole of the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *pat-, *paþa- (“to walk, tread, go, step”), of uncertain origin and relation.
Perhaps a blend of zanca (“leg”) + gamba (“leg”). Compare Sicilian ciampa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”). Compare English patten.
Inherited from Old Spanish farpa (“rag, shred”) influenced by zarria (“rag”).

Possibly from garfa (“animal's claw”), from Andalusian Arabic جَارْفَا (gárfa, “handful”), from Arabic غُرْفَة (ḡurfa, “cup or dipper”), from غَرَفَ (ḡarafa, “to ladle”), with influence from garfio (“hook”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *pata, fom Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”).
